Regarding the causes and conditions for Maitreya’s request to expound this Great Treatise, they are explained elsewhere.
Maitreya then spoke these root verses of the treatise.
It is titled the *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā*.
Once Asaṅga had received it,
he entrusted it to Vasubandhu, instructing him to compose a detailed commentary.
Therefore, this prose commentary composed by Vasubandhu is titled the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*.
"Vibhāga" (Discrimination) is a synonym for "manifesting" (*vibhāvita*) and "analyzing" (*vibhakta*).
"Middle" is a term for that which is correct, good, and free from extremes;
"extremes" is a designation for that which is erroneous, evil, and characterized by faults.
This is, in other words, a clear exposition of what is correct and what is erroneous.
If that is so, why are they not called "the deviant and the correct," but rather "the middle and the extremes"?
Now, the terms "middle and extremes" are used to reveal the Middle Way situated between them, which avoids the two types of extremist attachment and accords with the correct principle.
Therefore, this name is designated to distinguish it from the partial teachings of existence and the partial teachings of emptiness;
for although those are correct and wholesome, they are not the Middle Way.
Therefore, it is said "Middle and Extremes" rather than "Correct and Erroneous.
The term "Middle and Extremes" refers to the name of the principle being elucidated.
Furthermore, regarding "discourse" (*vāda*):
it refers to the capacity to manifest the title of the teaching;
that is, this treatise’s teaching clarifies correct and erroneous principles and fully distinguishes the Middle Way from the extremes.
The term "Madhyānta-vibhāga" (Discrimination of the Middle and the Extremes) is included within the sixth case-ending of the *sāmānādhikaraṇa* (co-ordinate) declension;
among the six types of *vigraha* (etymological analysis), it is an *upapada* (dependent) compound.
The old claim that this was composed by Vasubandhu is incorrect;
furthermore, the statement regarding the *Madhyāntavibhāga* does not accord with this [tradition].
Regarding the "Chapter on the Characteristics of Clouds" (*Yunxiang pin*): that which is expounded is termed the "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*),
which refers to the characteristics of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) clarified herein.
However, that which is elucidated therein is not merely the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
For instance, the verse of homage and the subsequent general introductory verse outlining the seven meanings are both not [mere] characteristics.
The chapter is named "Characteristics" (Lakṣaṇa-parivarta) because it establishes its title for the most part based on its subject matter,
just as the "Vehicle of No-Superior" (Anuttarayāna-parivarta) does;
so some explain.
Regarding the designations:
one should understand that the sequence, increase, and decrease of these seven categories are as follows.
However, the first two chapters concern the object;
the next three chapters concern the practice;
and the final two chapters concern the fruit.
These are the seven categories of intention.
Furthermore, the initial verses of homage were composed by Vasubandhu;
from this point onward, all the verses are spoken by Maitreya.
Maitreya’s original work consists of one hundred and thirteen verses;
the first verse provides a general summary,
and the last verse serves as a concluding explanation.
The middle section constitutes the main body of the treatise.
Vasubandhu’s commentary consists of seven hundred verses,
each composed of eight syllables, neither longer nor shorter.
Thirty-two characters constitute a verse (*śloka*).
However, before Vasubandhu had returned [to India],
fourteen characters constituted a single line of a verse.
Fifty-six characters constitute one verse;
this was already translated during the Liang dynasty by the former Paramārtha,
but its phrasing is erroneous and its meaning deviant.

Chapter One: On Characteristics (*Lakṣaṇa*). The Treatise says:
"I prostrate myself before the author of this treatise... and shall diligently manifest its meaning.
The commentary states:
This treatise, as a whole, consists of three parts.
The root verses of Maitreya consist of the main body of the treatise along with the concluding commentary;
herein, the first section is that which was spoken by Vasubandhu.
This is the first part: the introductory section of specific homage.
However, in various sūtras and śāstras, the practice of paying general homage to the Triple Gem is termed the "General Preface" (sāmānyanidāna),
yet this treatise lacks it.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on Great Wisdom), fascicle 64, and the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*, chapter 1:
Since this commentary explains the basis and the originator of this treatise by the two masters,
it omits the general introduction— the homage to the Triple Gem—
and proceeds directly to the specific introduction.
The meaning of the text is twofold.
The first three phrases constitute the homage to the specific teacher;
the fourth phrase reveals the intent of that homage.
The treatise shall now be composed.
Within the first three phrases,
the initial two characters manifest the characteristics of taking refuge and paying homage.
Next, these thirteen characters clarify the object of refuge and veneration.
As for the term "prostrate" (*kṣemaśiras*),
it refers to giving rise to a profound and pure mind and manifesting the three supreme types of action (*trikarma*).
This is another name for the expression of sincere refuge and reverent salutation.
"Kie" (稽) means "to reach";
"shu" (首) means "head."
Because one brings the hands to the head, it is called "bowing the head" (*kai-shu*).
This is the explanation provided by Confucianism.
Now, I shall also speak of the words while simultaneously urging the mental faculty (*manas-karma*).
"To cast oneself down in sincerity and request that [the name] be kept in mind" refers to prostration (*praṇāma*).
This term "prostration" applies generally to both objects of veneration;
within the context of those to whom one turns for refuge and respect, it is used here.
The first eight characters clearly manifest the Lord Maitreya, the master of this verse;
the following five characters clarify that the author of the treatise is the Bodhisattva Asaṅga.
Regarding the term "Sugata":
This refers to the fifth of the Tathāgata’s ten titles.
In Sanskrit it is called Sugata;
the older transcription "Xiujia'tuo" (修伽陀) is an error.
"Sū" is translated as "good" (śubha).
"Geya" means "one who has already passed away.
For now, it is abbreviated as "Sugata" (Well-Gone).
"Good" means excellent;
"departed" means gone.
If there were defiled evils arising within the cycle of birth and death, [one would not be called good and departed].
To purely maintain pure intention and depart well for nirvāṇa is precisely the Tathāgata’s enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) and transformation body (nirmāṇakāya);
or it is that the dharma-body (dharmakāya) has already departed well.
Therefore, the name "Sugata" (Well-Gone) is established;
it refers to one who is about to go well, rather than one who has already gone well.
Thus, one should say *suyāntu* (pronounced with a level tone as *yāntu*).
This is translated simply as "Gati" (Gone/Departed).
Alternatively, it carries the meaning of "going," which is a designation for one who possesses excellent progress while still in the causal stage.
It is not that the name "having gone well" is applied once the fruit is perfected.
As for the term "essence" (*tattva*) mentioned in the treatise,
it signifies the meaning of "nature" (*svabhāva*).
Alternatively, it has the meaning of "body" (*kāya*).
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that the meaning of "body" and the meaning of "substance" (*ātman*) are not distinct.
According to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis,
the essence of the Sugata is called the "Sugata-essence";
this essence is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The Sugata is precisely the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) and the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya).
If analyzed as a karmadhāraya compound,
it means that the essence itself is the Sugata, and thus it is called the "essence of the Sugata."
This essence of the Sugata is itself the other two bodies.
That is to say, the Venerable Maitreya—who is about to succeed to the rank of Buddha and is a true son of the Sugata—is called "born from that.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that this is the excellence of the Bodhisattva family.
This means he is one born and raised within the family of the Buddhas,
unlike the ignorant servant-children of the śrāvakas;
it is intended to manifest that the station of Maitreya is supremely exalted as a true son of the Tathāgata.
It is named after that which is produced from it;
alternatively, the true body of the Sugata is the Dharmakāya.
The Compassionate Honored One, the Awakened One, takes the Dharma as his father.
Only when taking suchness as an object does wisdom arise;
therefore, this Lord of Compassion is called the Son of the Sugata.
The old term "Son of Good Conduct" is incorrect.
To go forth is called "practice" (*caryā*).
However, the Sugata is not a mere track of practice.
Thus the Compassionate Honored One spoke in verse:
This refers to the master of the sūtras who composed this treatise;
therefore, one must pay homage to him.
For this reason, the treatise states: "I bow my head to the one born from the essence of the Sugata who composed this treatise."
He then paid his respects to the Venerable Maitreya and to our teacher,
the Bodhisattva Asaṅga, my elder brother Vasubandhu.
Having first received it from the venerable Maitreya, Asaṅga then taught it to Vasubandhu.
It was through his elder brother’s instruction that Vasubandhu composed the commentary.
Because Maitreya himself designated both himself and his disciples, he referred to them as "we."
This means that one regards one's elder brother as a teacher because he is able to instruct those such as oneself;
likewise, we now prostrate ourselves before our teacher who instructs us.
The three preceding phrases specifically pay homage to the two types of masters— the scriptures and the teachers.
"One should diligently clarify this meaning" indicates that,
having already paid homage with reverence, one shall now compose this treatise.
"Diligence" (*vīrya*) is a synonym for "exertion" (*vīrya*) and "valiance" (*parākrama*).
It reveals the absence of indolence and the capacity to subdue the enemy of the unwholesome.
"Valiance" clarifies the meaning of this root verse.

The commentary states:
This is a further presentation of the essential meaning.
Within this chapter, there are twenty-two verses;

The subsequent eleven verses analyze the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Now, since the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is entirely devoid of substantial reality, there is no separate verse to explain it;

Nevertheless, this nature exists due to false conceptualization and the like;
now, within this context, it is also understood through the non-existence [of that nature].
Within the first eleven verses, there are two [sections].
First, the nine characteristics are explained individually;
below, they are summarized.
Within the eleven verses explaining these individual characteristics:
The first two verses distinguish the existence and non-existence of the three natures based on false discrimination (*vikalpa*).
The next two verses distinguish the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of false discrimination.

Next, there is one verse that analyzes the characteristic of origination.
Next, there are two verses that analyze the characteristic of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
This verse and the following one analyze the characteristics of existence and non-existence.
This verse correctly explains the characteristics of existence and non-existence;
the subsequent verse concludes by definitively establishing existence and non-existence,
thereby clarifying the characteristic of the Middle Way.

The Commentary states:
In this section, each passage first restates the text and subsequently elaborates upon its meaning:
the grasper and the grasped are the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), while the conceptualization that takes these as its object is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Because it is that which can be the object of cognition and is not something grasped [as a substantial entity],
and because it is not entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
it is called "existent."
This refers to the discrimination between the grasped object and the grasping subject;
it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound for its name,
rather than a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) designation based on the identity of the two graspings and the discrimination itself.

However, this is stated solely with reference to the defiled portion; it means that false discrimination exists as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), not that within the dependent nature there is only false discrimination.
This is because pure discrimination also exists as the dependent nature.
The Treatise says:

The Commentary states:

However, even according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, there is still the arising of attachment toward the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Question: As it is stated in the treatise...

The Commentary states:

that is to say, if within this false discrimination those two types of grasping do not exist.

Within that false discrimination, there is also that suchness;

These two natures are the substance remaining after the two grasps; because they are not non-existent, one knows them as they truly are to exist.
That is to say, in other treatises it is known that there is existence;

The commentary states:
The first two lines clarify that the objects transformed by deluded discrimination have a dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).

The old [translation] states: "The fundamental consciousness gives rise to that which resembles the sense organs, objects, self, and consciousness. This is not so. Why is this?

If one were to allow such transformation,
it would contradict the prose commentary of that earlier treatise.
The prose auto-commentary explains:
"That which resembles a self" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it is associated with the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and so forth.
Regarding that which "resembles consciousness," this refers to the six types of consciousness; yet even this is not [the case].
One should rather say that it is transformed into the object of cognition.
That which is cognized refers to the six objects,

The Chinese text can be understood according to its literal phrasing.
Within it, in each case, the two extremes are first described,
followed by the exposition of the Middle Way.
This refers to non-Buddhists and others who maintain that the five aggregates, such as form and so forth, are distinct from the self;
this is the conception of a self as being separate from the aggregates,
or alternatively, as being identical to them.
To conceive of a self within the aggregates is called one extreme;
thus, two extremes are established.
The treatise says:
"To abandon this attachment, up to and including [the term] 'Māṇava'.
The commentary states:
"This is to abandon the dualistic extremes of difference and identity."
Therefore, in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, the Buddha taught the Middle Way,
which is said to be the contemplation of [the absence of self] from the person (*pudgala*) down to the youth (*māṇava*). That is to say,
it extends through six categories up to the "middle."
There are eight types in total:
first, the self;
second, sentient beings.
Third, those who give life;
fourth, those who provide birth;
fifth, those who nurture and raise.
Sixth, the *pudgala*;
seventh, the *manomaya* (mind-born);
eighth, the *māṇava*.
"Maṇava" refers to the "Child of the Sages" (Māṇavaka).
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 83,
the treatise says:
Seeing that there is a self, or that it is identical to the body.
The commentary states:
this explains the reason why.
There are two types of fixed positions regarding whether the self and the aggregates are identical or distinct,
as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Since these two are combined to form the third [alternative],
and since neither a self nor a "person" (pudgala) exists,
how could it be either different from or identical to the aggregates?
The first of the two extremes above is concluded.
From here below is the second.
The treatise says:
If one regards form and so forth as being ultimate, this is the extreme of the śrāvakas.
The commentary states:
Among the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), there are those who cling to the notion that things are not eternal.
As in the case of the *Vaiśeṣika* and other schools,
it is spoken of as "eternal" from the perspective of its predominant state; therefore, it is simply called "constant."
The Treatise says:
"In order to abandon this attachment, [it is stated that it is] neither permanent nor impermanent.
The Commentary states:
Since that which is grasped does not exist, there is neither permanence nor impermanence.
Furthermore, the form of the dharma-nature is not impermanent,
and the form dependent on others is not permanent.
Therefore, combining these two natures, one speaks of "neither permanent nor impermanent.
While the substance of form may exist, it cannot be described as either form or non-form;
whereas the substance of the self is entirely non-existent, such that one can only say that the characteristic of the self is absent.
From here below is the third section, the explanation of the two extremes.
The treatise says:
"From the fixed attachment that there is a self up to the extreme of deprecating sentient beings."
The commentary states:
This describes the adherence to a real self (*ātman*).
Since there is no time when one does not cling to a self, how could there be the fault of deprecation (*apavāda*)?
The Treatise says:
"They also negate the conventional existence of sentient beings.
The Commentary states:
This explains the reason.

If one merely clings to the non-existence of a substantial self, although this is not a deprecation [of reality], it is like the view of emptiness held by non-Buddhist outsiders and by masters such as Bhāviveka, who establish the negation of the conventional self.
Therefore, it constitutes a denial [of existence].
This is the commentator’s explanation of the intent behind that [opponent's] position.
The treatise says:

"To depart from this attachment and reach the wisdom that abides in the middle between the two extremes" means to abide in the wisdom that dwells in the middle between the two extremes of self and non-self.
That is to say, one neither dogmatically clings to the existence of a real self nor to the existence of a conventional self;
rather, one understands them in accordance with the teachings,
thereby achieving "middle knowledge."
This constitutes the second pair regarding sentient beings.
Next, the two aspects of phenomena are distinguished;
this is the fourth pair of extremes.
The Treatise says:
"One dogmatically clings to the mind as having real existence until one reaches the extreme of the diminution of phenomena.
The Commentary states:
This is a description of speculative views.
Since all phenomena are primarily "mind-only," the term "mind" alone is used here to refer to the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
There are many varieties of such attachments that hold phenomena to have real existence.
The grasping of phenomena as having reality is like the views of non-Buddhists such as Bhāviveka;
however, the phenomena as they are grasped lack reality,
whereas phenomena in their dependent nature possess reality.
Therefore, it cannot be said [that they exist],
because they also negate the conventional nature of phenomena.
Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), a real self (*ātman*) does not exist.
Therefore, since they are not of the same nature,
one must employ the provisional expression "resembling a self.
The treatise says:
"To abandon this attachment, one reaches the state of being without mind and without consciousness.
The commentary states:
"Without mind" refers to the eighth consciousness.
"Mind" refers to the seventh consciousness;
"consciousnesses" refers to the other six.
These constitute the sovereign mind (citta-rāja).
Among the mental factors (*caitta*), only volition (*cetanā*) is mentioned because its activity is preeminent;
by this example, the other mental factors are implied.
Thus, there are no grasped dharmas of mind or mental factors.
Therefore, there are no dharmas that are either real or unreal;
however, because they exist as real dharmas within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
it is not the same as my [position].
This causes them to abide in middle knowledge;
this constitutes the second [aspect] of the Dharma.
Below this, the fifth section distinguishes the two extremes.
The Treatise says:
"From the adherence to the existence of unwholesome [dharmas] up to this point, these are the counteractive applications.
The Commentary states:
This is a description of the misconception.
The treatise says:
"In order to abandon this misconception, one does not follow [others'] exhortations or praises."
The commentary states:
"Not following" means not following along with defilement or purity to give rise to grasping.
"Not exhorting" means not exhorting others to cling to the distinction between defilement and purity.
"Not praising" means...
One does not praise or explain defilement and purity so as to cause others to believe, hear, and give rise to fixed attachments;
thus, the single character "not" (bu) runs through all three characters.
As the Old Treatise says:
It does not go and it does not come; there is no coming, no analogy, and no speech.
"Going" refers to following;
"coming" refers to exhortation.
The term "for example" (*pīti*) means "praise.
From here below is the sixth section, which distinguishes the two extremes.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the phenomena of sentient beings, this refers to the limit of their cessation and diminution.
The Commentary states:
It is by grasping at the present and the future as existing that one conceives of them as eternal;
it is by grasping at the future as non-existent that one clings to annihilationism.
Therefore, existence and non-existence are used to reveal the delusions of eternalism and annihilationism.
"Permanence" involves grasping;
"annihilation" is without grasping.
The treatise says:
"To depart from this attachment and reach the wisdom that lies between the two extremes.
Commentary: Since truly existent dharmas do not exist, [the extremes are abandoned].
Therefore, it is neither eternal nor annihilated.
Although things exist in dependence upon others, they are likewise neither eternal nor annihilated.
Thus, the Buddha merely taught that one should abide in middle-way wisdom.
That which is grasped does not exist;
yet that which is dependent is not non-existent.
From here below, the seventh [section] distinguishes between the two extremes.
The Treatise says:
"To cling to the existence of ignorance and to cling to the existence of clarity are each an extreme.
The Commentary states:
The twelve factors of defilement and purification each have two aspects;
the same applies to the two appropriations within the pure dependent origination.
These all take ignorance as their primary cause.
"Clarity" refers to untainted clarity (*anāsrava-vidyā*).
The treatise states:
"Thus, the adherence to existence up to the path of counteraction each constitutes an extreme."
The commentary states:
The same applies to the remaining eleven members regarding the relationship between the antidotes and their objects, as well as the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).
Among these, all that serve as antidotes are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because it is described as being capable of grasping;
if the unconditioned were not capable of such grasping activity,
then among the remedies, the term "unconditioned" would not be mentioned.
Because it is not produced by karma or afflictions,
and because it is not subject to arising, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus, according to the Abhidharma, the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) encompasses both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
This concludes the seventh section, which summarizes the various speculative views.
Next, the two meanings are consolidated.
The treatise states:
"From these objects of treatment up to the distinctions of the white category.
The commentary states:
These twelve links, beginning with ignorance, are the objects of treatment.
This refers to the factors of the dark category (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, which serve as the antidotes;
it refers to the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) of the white category (*śuklapakṣa*).
What is clarified here is precisely what is taught elsewhere regarding the dark and white categories.
The Treatise says:
"In order to abandon this attachment," and so forth, as explained at length.
The Commentary states:
In clarity there is neither duality nor two parts;
in ignorance there is likewise neither duality nor two parts.
That there is no duality means that there is no dual essence.
"Non-dual" means that it cannot be separated into two distinct parts.
The textual meaning of the remaining eleven links is identical.
Therefore, the treatise says, "and so forth," providing a detailed explanation according to the sequence of that sutra;
this is extensively present in the current *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other works.
Now, the treatise continues as follows:
The treatise says:
"Because [states] such as clarity and ignorance are all ultimately non-existent.
The commentary states:
Because within clarity there is no duality of grasped and grasper,
how could there be duality or the two parts?
This is the commentator’s interpretation of the meaning of the sūtra.
The first fascicle of the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* also contains this interpretation.
From here below is the eighth section, which distinguishes the two extremes (*antadvaya*).
The treatise states:
"There are three types of affliction, up to the affliction of birth.
Commentary: This is intended to explain the two extremes.
First, the two dharmas of defilement and purity based on the dependent nature are discussed;
therein, defilement is treated first, followed by purity.
This enumerates the names of the three defilements;
from here on, each shall be explained in detail.
The treatise says:
"From the defilement of afflictions up to the aspiration for a third subsequent existence.
Commentary: This separately explains the three types of defilement.
Among these, there are two pairs:
first that which is to be remedied, and subsequently that which is the remedy.
This refers to that which is to be remedied.
Regarding all views, they are all views of the path of cultivation;
as for the characteristics of greed, hatred, and delusion,
these three are the roots from which the rest arise.
It is not that pride, doubt, the fetters, or the secondary afflictions lack characteristics;
rather, they all involve grasping at characteristics.
It is simply for this reason that these alone are cited.
However, the ten types of augmented characteristics, such as form and sound, are not afflictions;
therefore, they are not discussed here.
That which follows is the craving for renewed existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*).
However, as for the essence of this craving,
its substance consists of the two dharmas of greed and desire,
because it seeks to defile oneself.
However, taking craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) alone as its essence is also logically uncontradictory;
the former two are present defiled afflictions.
The third is attachment to future afflictions;
this is craving for renewed existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*),
or craving for the three evil destinies (*durgati*).
The noble ones do not give rise to craving for the meditative attainments;
however, they do give rise to craving for future existence in the happy realms.
The Treatise says:
"This antidote extends up to the knowledge of wishlessness.
The Commentary states:
This illustrates three types of afflictions that can be remedied:
emptiness eliminates various views, such as the view of a self and what belongs to a self,
because emptiness is capable of removing them.
The signless [samādhi] can eliminate the signs of greed, hatred, and delusion;
the wishless wisdom can remedy all wishes for future existence,
because one no longer seeks or aspires within the three realms.
Because during the stage of preparation one separately cultivates emptiness and so forth as specific antidotes for the views and so forth,
although all three types are abandoned collectively in a single moment upon reaching the fundamental stage,
it is said that they are abandoned individually for the sake of the underlying meaning.
These three types may be designated simply as "emptiness" and so forth;
they encompass both meditative concentration (*samāhita*) and non-concentrated states (*asamāhita*), as well as both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom.
Alternatively, they may be termed the "three samādhis," such as the samādhi of emptiness and so on.
Only the concentrated mind (samāhita-citta) possesses the untainted (anāsrava);
alternatively, it is simply called the three gates of liberation (trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni).
Only the untainted state is exclusively the concentrated mind.
Since it is not stated here that [this practice] consists of *samādhi* and so forth,
it encompasses both concentration and distraction, as well as both the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the two gates of suppression and abandonment.
However, the practice of the Middle Way is exclusively untainted and consists solely of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Because neither the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) nor other paths or other knowledges can sever it.
As for the term "liberation" (*vimukti*) mentioned in the old treatise,
it does not exist in the Sanskrit original.
The Treatise says:
"From the defilement of karma up to the knowledge of non-action.
The Commentary states:
Second, regarding the defilement of karma (*karmasaṃkleśa*), the factors to be remedied (*vipakṣa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*) each constitute one type.
Although these pertain to both the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the fundamental stage (*maula*), they do not actually produce [karma];
rather, they are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) and do not perform action.
Because karma does not arise.
The treatise says:
"The defilement of birth extends to the continuity of the third future existence."
The commentary states:
The third [type] is the defilement of birth.
The first [point] refers generally to the stage at the time of the initial birth toward a future existence (*punarbhava*).
The second [moment] is discussed in terms of the first moment of birth;
the third is discussed in terms of the entire period.
The former three are distinct, while the latter one is comprehensive.
Therefore, these three types neither decrease nor increase.
The Treatise says:
This is the wisdom of non-intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) that serves as the antidote.
The commentary states:
One should understand that these three are to be assigned in their respective order.
However, the wisdom of right abandonment is exclusively non-conceptual and takes true suchness as its object.
Since the objects to be remedied (*pratipakṣya*)— such as non-arising and so forth— are distinct,
the discussion concerns the capacity of the initial remedy; thus,
the differences among the remedies are explained.
If there is no hindrance during the stage of application (*prayoga*), they are likewise suppressed;
this specifically reveals the three objects to be remedied,
while the following passage reveals them collectively.
The Treatise says:
"These three kinds are explained as being pure.
The Commentary states:
There are three types of objects to be remedied, and likewise three types of remedies.
This explains that within the two categories of defilement and purity, there are three of each;
these pure remedies are precisely the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
If that which is the basis of purification is itself suchness,
yet the previous discussion stated that the counteragent consists solely of true gnosis,
the intention here is as follows:
One can infer accordingly.
The treatise says:
"The objects of knowledge for emptiness and so forth refer to phenomena such as emptiness."
The commentary states:
In order to explain that grasping at purity constitutes one extreme,
it first presents the essence of purity.
This refers to the knowledge of emptiness, the knowledge of signlessness, the knowledge of wishlessness, and the knowledge of non-action,
as well as the objects of the three knowledges of non-arising and so forth—
namely, the dharmas such as emptiness.
Phenomena such as emptiness are precisely *tathatā* (suchness),
which is termed "emptiness," "wishlessness," and so forth, up to "lack of intrinsic nature.
With emptiness as the primary one, there are six other such types.
The Treatise says:
"The three kinds of affliction lead to making [them] empty, and so forth.
The Commentary states:
When the three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) are to be abandoned as appropriate,
it is not by means of the seven knowledges such as emptiness that these three afflictions are made empty and so forth; rather,
it is according to what is appropriate.
That is to say, it is not the wisdom of emptiness that causes things to be empty;
it is not the wisdom of signlessness that causes things to be signless;
and so on, up to it is not the wisdom of the absence of intrinsic nature that causes things to be without intrinsic nature.
It is not the case that each [wisdom] acts as a distinct basis by severing its respective object through its specific antidote;
therefore, it is said that they act according to what is appropriate, rather than making them empty and so forth.
The "wisdoms such as emptiness" (śūnyatā-ādi-jñāna) include the other six wisdoms.
The phrase "those who posit emptiness and so forth" includes the remaining six types, namely those who posit the signless and so on. Why is this?
Because they maintain that after the three defilements have ceased, there exists emptiness and the like.
Because [the treatise] treats the cessation of defilements as being "emptiness" and so forth,
it is stated here in the treatise that it is not those [defilements] themselves that cause [it] to be made so.
For what reason is it not caused to be produced by that?
The treatise says:
Because its intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) and ultimate nature (*dharmatā*) are untainted.
The commentary states:

Because the intrinsic nature of those three defilements is precisely such dharmas as emptiness, and because that nature is the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and the original nature of the dharma-realm is undefiled.
Their nature is inherently empty, inherently signless, and so on, up to being inherently selfless and lacking intrinsic nature.
It is not by means of the wisdom of emptiness and so forth that the three types of defilement are only now made empty, signless, and so on.
The preceding sections have already concluded the exposition that both defilement and purification each consist of three aspects,
as well as the exposition on the true principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The treatise states:
"If [it is argued that] within the dharma-realm there is neither defilement nor purity.
Commentary: This describes a speculative position.
The fundamental nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is entirely free from defilement;
this is precisely the meaning of its being primordially pure by nature.
If one were to maintain that it was defiled at a prior time and subsequently became pure and stainless, [that would be a misconception].
Because it is newly produced.
The two attachments to defilement and purity each constitute an extreme.
The treatise says:
"To abandon this attachment," and so forth, as explained at length.
The commentary states:
"That is to say, it is not by means of emptiness."
It is not by means of the knowledge of emptiness that one is able to empty phenomena;
it is by means of being able to empty all views regarding phenomena.
"Phenomenal nature is itself empty" means that the intrinsic nature of all views and defilements is emptiness.
This is the explanation.
It is not by means of the wisdom of emptiness that phenomena are made empty;
this is the intended meaning here.
For example, when one perceives emptiness, it is not by means of the wisdom of emptiness that what is perceived is made empty.
It causes those various views to become empty once again,
because the nature of phenomena is by its very nature empty. If,
through the wisdom of emptiness, one brings about the severance of all views, it reveals that the emptiness of views is primordially present.
Since it is acceptable that what was previously defiled subsequently relies upon emptiness,
as in the previous position,
this is now stated to be an extreme.
When this principle is revealed, that which can counteract those attachments is called the practice of the Middle Way.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth, explained at length":
this refers to the detailed explanation of signlessness (*animitta*) up to the wisdom of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-jñāna*).
It can cause the continuity of future existence to arise; likewise, it can cause future existence not to continue.
The first two verses have already been explained above.
Below, the final two lines of the verses will be explained.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, there are seven kinds of conceptualization regarding the two extremes.
The Commentary states:
Explaining the first two lines of the third verse:
this is also from the *Ratnakūṭa*,
and as it is the same scripture as the preceding one, it is not presented separately.
The Treatise says:
What are the seven?
The Commentary states:
This section specifically investigates the seven [factors].
Below, each is answered individually.
The treatise states:
This means that the conceptualization of existence and non-existence each constitutes an extreme.
The commentary states:
"This describes the two types of extremist attachments."
It has not yet been revealed what kind of entity this is, nor by what cause that grasping at a self-body arises.
The treatise says:
That grasping [at a self] is held to be truly existent, ranging from the conceptualized to the unconditioned.
The commentary states:
That [view] is the adherence to real existence;
the term *pudgala* reveals the essence of what is adhered to.
The phrase "because he considers [it] to be destroyed" clarifies the basis for his attachment.
Why does he cling to the existence of a *pudgala* (person)?
Since the Buddha, the World-Honored One, established emptiness for the purpose of destroying this [notion of intrinsic nature],
if this were non-existent in essence— like the hair of a tortoise—
for what phenomenon would he have to destroy in order to establish emptiness as the basis for that destruction?
Since both existence and emptiness exist,
they must depend on something for their cessation;
therefore, the essence of that which is ceased is certainly not non-existent.
This reveals the reason for the adherence to existence; or,
one may conceptually construct non-self as being non-existent,
which reveals the cause for the adherence to non-existence.
If that which is extinguished by the meditative absorption on emptiness were truly existent,
then the essence of the self and phenomena being extinguished would not be definitively non-existent.
If the essence of the self were non-existent, [how could it be extinguished?]
The selfless (anātman) should not exist,
because that which is its opposite is absent,
just like the horns of a rabbit and so forth.
Because that which is to be remedied does not exist,
that which remedies it also does not exist;
that which is remedied by me does not exist.
The absence of self should be likewise.
If there were such a thing as the absence of self,
then the self would not be non-existent.
Since the self is non-existent,
that which is "non-self" does not exist either.
Thus, the relationship between the object of treatment and the agent of treatment is established with certainty through existence and non-existence.
Therefore, the irrationality of maintaining [the existence of] a self lies herein.
To establish this through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is said:
"The self that is the object of negation exists."
Because there are remedies for them.
Just as there are three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*),
these three remedies are said to exist as previously described.
He establishes the Cloud of Immeasurability.
Selflessness does not exist as a substantial entity,
because there is nothing to be remedied.
Like the horns of a rabbit and so forth,
this self, when contrasted with non-self,
involves the grasping at existence and the grasping at non-existence; it differs from the aforementioned extreme views of augmentation and diminution.
The treatise says:
"In order to be free from such [faults], up to and including the full exposition.
The commentary states:
This negates what is clung to as non-empty, for it is empty from the very beginning;
it is not that I first establish the emptiness of the three time periods by means of destroying a self.
By this, it is revealed that the self is definitively non-existent and that non-self exists.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth, as explained at length," the treatise states:
"From the conceptualization of that which is to be pacified up to each being an extreme."
The commentary states:
This describes the second extreme.
The treatise says:
Because one clings to that which is to be abandoned and thus fears emptiness.
[The commentary] states:
That which is to be abandoned is that which is to be pacified.
"That which is capable of cutting off is that which is capable of pacifying.
This reveals the nature of what is grasped.
For what reason does such a grasping arise?
Because they fear emptiness;
fearing that what is to be abandoned might be abandoned, they apprehend an emptiness that could effect such cessation.
It is because of this fear of emptiness.
This refers to the attachment to the two types of tranquility (*śānti*).
The treatise says:
"In order to abandon such [attachments], it proceeds to explain the analogy of space."
The commentary states:
Regarding the scriptural metaphors for emptiness,
it is like a person who, out of fear of this space, abandons it and flees, only to find that another space has arrived.
They are all deluded.
This case is likewise:
that which is tranquilized and that which tranquilizes are fundamentally empty from the very beginning.
What is there to fear?
That which is severed and abandoned results in the attainment of tranquil emptiness.
The treatise says:
"Differentiating what is feared leads to each becoming an extreme.
Commentary: This describes the third extreme.
The conceptualization of what is feared constitutes one [extreme],
and the conceptualization of the terrifying phenomena arising from that source constitutes another;
thus, two extremes are established.
The essential nature [of the parikalpita] and its cause have not yet been revealed.
The treatise says:
"Because one clings to the existence of the parikalpita, it leads to the arising of fear."
The commentary states:
Herein, the fear arising from conceptual construction is generally revealed;
the apprehended forms and so forth reveal the nature of that which is feared.
Because fear can arise, the reason for this clinging is revealed:

namely, that if one definitively clings to the perceived objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, these become the cause for the miserable realms (*apāya*), and one will consequently be born in those miserable realms.
Therefore, the perceived form is truly something from which fear can arise.
If all bodhisattvas fear that form is without reality,
what is it that they fear?
The treatise says:
"Because one who clings to existence [clings] to that from which fear arises.
The commentary states:
"In this context, it is shown in general that conceptualization gives rise to that which is fearful."
The phenomena of suffering that arise manifest the essence of what is to be feared;
because they can give rise to fear, they manifest the basis for grasping.

That is to say, the phenomena of suffering—such as the oppression of the miserable realms—that arise from grasping at form and so forth, are capable of generating fear because these oppressive phenomena can produce dread.
If one realizes suffering as empty, how could fear arise?
The treatise says:
To abandon such [fear], it proceeds to explain the analogy of the painter.
The commentary states:
Regarding the analogy of the painter,
it refers to a certain ignorant painter who exists in the world.
It is like a painting of a terrifying yakṣa;
instead of being able to seize weapons and inflict harm upon oneself, one is rather terrified by it.
This case is just the same.
Having transformed oneself into that form,
one instead fears it because it can lead to rebirth in the miserable realms (durgati) and the resulting suffering and oppression.
The treatise says:
The preceding analogy of space was taught for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
The commentary states:
the two analogies of quiescent emptiness were taught for the sake of the śrāvakas.
This is because they are excessively attached to existence and thus fear emptiness.
This analogy of the painter represents the bodhisattva,
who is excessively attached to emptiness and thus fears existence.
Since the two types of tranquility are originally empty, why fear emptiness?
Since form and the other aggregates have self-origination,
why fear existence?
The Treatise says:
"The conceptualization of the grasped object up to each being a single extreme.
The Commentary states:
To describe the fourth side:
among the previous eight sides,
the first consists of the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*) of both the defiled and the pure aspects of grasping.
This refers to all forms of dualistic grasping;

The meaning of "separation from birth" (*visamyoga*) and so forth is explained as in the first volume of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The treatise states:
"Because the six [perfections] are accomplished through the cultivation and realization of sentient beings over a long period of accumulation."
The commentary states:
Because firm roots of goodness have been accumulated over a long period of time,
one cultivates and realizes this [state] in order to bring sentient beings to maturity.
These roots of goodness, being difficult to destroy, are called "firm roots of goodness.
The Commentary states:
Because the mind has become pliant through the cultivation and realization of the seven purities of the Buddha-land.
The commentary states:
Through the mind becoming pliant and supple, one cultivates and realizes the Pure Land.
As Vimalakīrti said:
"Because the mind is pure, the Buddha-field is pure.
The Commentary says:
"This refers to the eighth stage, the stage of non-retrogression, where one receives the prediction and cultivates realization until reaching the point of no longer being subject to regression."
The commentary states:
"Those who receive a prediction" refers to receiving a prediction from the Buddha;
"those who do not regress" is explained by the treatise itself.
Because they do not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa,
and because they are not subject to regression from these two states,
they differ from ordinary beings who regress and enter back into saṃsāra.
Unlike the lesser sages who regress and enter into nirvana,
because they do not regress, they cultivate and realize non-retrogression; furthermore,
they realize and receive the prediction [of enlightenment], and there are two kinds of such predictions.
Because the predictions received over the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* each differ.
The treatise says:
"In the nine Buddha-stages, cultivation and realization are non-dual because of the absence of the two obstacles."
The treatise says:
"Tenth, because the cultivation and realization of manifest enlightenment proceed without rest.
The commentary says:
Because the activities for the benefit and happiness of others proceed without cessation, one cultivates and realizes that manifestation of enlightenment.
Among these ten [categories], the first is the innate lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*),
while from the second onwards they are called the acquired lineage (*samudānīta-gotra*).
The third is the entry into the first eon;
the fourth is the practice of the various stages of the path;
and the fifth is the path of seeing.
The sixth is the path of cultivation up to the seventh stage.
The seventh is the characteristic of the eighth stage,
because of mastery over the buddha-field.
The eighth is [the stage of] the ninth and tenth grounds,
because it is proximate to the Buddha-ground and because non-abiding nirvana is fully perfected therein.
Although the eighth [ground] attains mastery over the land for the first time,
it is described from the perspective of its excellence.
The ninth is the dharma-body and the self-enjoyment body.
The tenth consists of the enjoyment body for others (*parasaṃbhoga-kāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).
Because the conditions are unimpeded and so forth,
their spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is able to be cultivated and realized.
Therefore, as long as one has not yet entered [the path], it is not yet called cultivation or realization.
The above concludes the second major section of this chapter.
The treatise says:
Regarding the general meaning of the Unsurpassed Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*), [the text] proceeds to the meaning of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
The commentary states:
From this point downward is the main body of this chapter.
The third section is the summary of the above.
This constitutes three summaries in total.
The Treatise says:
"Because the correct practice is unsurpassed, it reaches the unsurpassed fruit of correct practice.
The commentary states:
There are six types of correct practice.
This is explained in detail as previously stated.
"Right practice" (samyak-pratipatti) is a designation established through the function of being unsurpassed;
for the right practice of the two vehicles cannot surpass it.
"Right practice" refers to the twelve objects of focus (*ālambana*).
"Object of focus" means "unsurpassed," and this is an instance of the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
Alternatively, that which is the object of focus for supreme practice is called "supreme in terms of its object" (*ālambanānuttarya*);
this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive) compound.
That which is superior to other objects is called "supreme in terms of its object."
This is called the practice of right conduct.
Right conduct is that which takes an object;
the twelve [links] are its objects.
To maintain the object so as not to forget it is called "maintaining through right practice" (*samyak-pratipatti-dhāraṇa*);
alternatively, it is so named because right practice arises by means of this method.
Because one maintains right practice, it is called "maintaining right practice" (*samyakpratipatti-dhāraṇa*).
The fruit of right practice is called "the fruit of right practice," which is also explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
Its essence is without cultivation or realization.
Cultivation and realization that are unsurpassed are termed "unsurpassed cultivation and realization.
As for what is called the "fruit," it refers to realizing the subsequent dharma by having cultivated the preceding causes;
this is what is designated as the fruit.
It is not necessary that only the fulfillment of the state of Buddhahood be termed the "fruit.
However, in the older treatise, the concluding text follows the section on the names in the commentary;
this is not without its own consistency.
The Treatise says:
For what reason is this treatise titled *Madhyāntavibhāga*?
The Commentary states:
From here on begins the third major section of the treatise,
which explains the "Section on the Bestowal of Vows.
This concludes the inquiry.
The verse of the treatise says:
"This treatise elucidates the Middle and the Extremes; may it eliminate all inauspiciousness.
The commentary states:
However, regarding this elucidation of the middle that is free from the two extremes,

in the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other texts, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu explains the two characters "middle" (*madhya*) and "extreme" (*anta*) within the first sentence through three successive turnings.
This shall be understood below.
Regarding the two meanings and the four sides of the characters,
the treatise says:
This treatise is able to analyze the meaning of reaching and being the object of cognition.
The commentary states:
"Analysis" means to clarify and manifest.
This is a dual explanation of the meaning of the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for both the middle way and the two extremes.
The "object-condition" and the "activity" (*caryā*) are combined and termed "the activity of the object-condition.
This is because there are activities that are not object-conditions.
Furthermore, for instance, false discrimination, hindrances, and so forth constitute the practice of the two extremes;
the practice within this [middle way] that is the opposite of these is called "practice.
It does not arise in isolation but necessarily takes an object as its condition.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, this [consciousness] is capable of discerning the object to which it reaches.
The Commentary states:
This section provides a dual analysis of the objects of focus (*ālambana*) regarding both extremes and the middle:
the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and so forth are the objects of the extremes,
while the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are the objects of the middle.
Therefore, when an activity conditions an object,
their conjunction is termed a "cause," which necessarily entails something apprehended.
Since what is obtained includes both good and evil,
this treatise does not clarify the results of evil;
it clarifies only the results of good.
Because the evil results were not mentioned, the name was not explained based on the intermediate results;
however, in the commentary on the treatise, the results are indeed clarified.
Furthermore, the results obtained in the middle are precisely what is explained in the third interpretation.
The Treatise says:
"Alternatively, because this correctly elucidates the 'reaching' (prāpti), it is called the *Madhyāntavibhāga*.
The Commentary states:
The first two interpretations both discuss the Middle and the Extremes;
now, this third [interpretation] concerns only the Middle without extremes,
as it correctly elucidates the Middle Way that is free from extremes— the Dharma of the Middle among middles.
This also distinguishes the results of the extreme dharmas,
or alternatively, it distinguishes the causes of the extremes;
as in the two previous interpretations, this constitutes the third explanation for the three characters "Middle" (madhya), "Extreme" (anta), and "Discrimination" (vibhāga) within the verse.
In the older treatise, the first three meanings appear before the verse;
this was an error by the translators.
What is meant by the dharma that is free from extremes and abides in the middle?
The Treatise says:
Because this treatise elucidates that which reaches the sphere of practice.
The Commentary says:
The arguments expounded in this treatise penetrate all four lower vehicles;
they are not the objects of investigation for ordinary beings,
nor are they the objects of reflection for those of the two vehicles.

It is called "profoundly secret" because it is not that which is sought by the *vitarka* (applied thought) of the desire realm or the first dhyāna, nor by the *cetanā* (volition) of the higher stages, nor that which is sought by the six consciousnesses or that which is thought by the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses].
"Profound" (*gambhīra*) carries the meaning of being deep and remote.
"Esoteric" (mi) means hidden meaning;
it is not something that can be known by those of shallow intelligence.
The treatise says:
This is because its meaning is solid and firm, and thus it cannot be overcome by them.
The commentary states:
It is like a vajra, which can shatter that which is not indestructible.
Therefore, it is called "solid and substantial.
By understanding this treatise, one is able to overcome others and cannot be subdued by them.
The treatise says:
"This is because the meaning of 'vast' extends to the welfare of both oneself and others.
The commentary states:
One’s own extensive benefit for others is great happiness;
others’ extensive happiness is one’s own great benefit;
or there is the extensive great benefit and happiness of both self and others.
Alternatively, "extensive" (vaipulya) refers to manifesting oneself [in vast forms],
while "great" (mahat) refers to surpassing others;
the meaning of "benefit and happiness" is as commonly understood.
The treatise says:
"Because all these meanings reach the three vehicles of the Dharma.
The commentary states:
The Great [Vehicle] contains all lesser meanings;
it fully elucidates and brings definitive resolution to the teachings of the three vehicles.
Therefore, it is called "all" because it encompasses everything that can be explained.
The Treatise says:
"Furthermore, it can eliminate [afflictions] up to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The Commentary states:
Explaining the fourth line of the verse:
The two obscurations cause one to transmigrate through birth and death and prevent the arising of wisdom and vision;
thus, they are termed "inauspicious."
If one understands this teaching and realizes this principle,
both [the afflictive and cognitive] obstructions can be simultaneously eliminated, whereby one is able to attain Buddhahood.
This concludes the general explanation of the title of the treatise.
The old commentary further includes the final two verses of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*,
yet upon examining three versions of the Sanskrit original, these are not present in any of them;
they were added by the translator.
The Treatise says:
"I have expounded the various merits of this treatise [so that one] may swiftly realize the vast and great *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Commentary states:
From this point downward, he makes a vow to dedicate the merit to sentient beings.
The first line clearly reveals the merit of the World-Honored One’s own commentary on the verse,
so that the lamp of the Dharma shall not be extinguished, the darkness of delusion shall be dispelled, and [suffering] shall not arise.
The Ten Powers bestow their secret empowerment,
and the eight classes of beings arouse reverence;
all of this elucidates the virtues arising from the original verses.
The second phrase clearly elucidates the dedication of merit.
"All" (xian) means every one;
"to hold" (chi) means to employ.
"Universal" (pu) means equal.
"Giving" (shi) means to rescue.
"The multitudes of beings" (qunsheng) refers to sentient beings.
The categories are not uniform.
This means that all the merits described in the root verses are employed to equally deliver all sentient beings;
the third line causes them to obtain the retribution of the cause.
The Bodhisattva’s six perfections consist of two kinds of paths:
the first three constitute the path for attaining higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*),
while the latter three constitute the path for attaining definitive excellence (*naiḥśreyasa*).
Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one attains the status of the ten kings.
While still at the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), one attains birth in superior states through the three previous attainments of the path of exalted rebirth (*abhyudaya-mārga*).
Through diligence and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), merit and stability are made preeminent.
The single perfection of *prajñā* brings about the excellence of wisdom and meditative concentration;
the latter three perfections result in the attainment of the definitive, supreme path.
By bestowing these upon all sentient beings, they enable them to attain these two fruits while still at the stage of a cause.
The fourth phrase causes one to obtain the fruition.
"Swiftly" means quickly;
"realization" means to accord with.
"Vast" (guǎng) means expansive;
"great" (dà) means profound.
In Sanskrit, it is called *bodhitattva*.
"Bodhi" means awakening (*bodha*).
"Traini" means three (*tri*).
This means that those of indeterminate lineage within the three vehicles each obtain the fruit of their own vehicle according to their respective inclinations.
The phrase "able to transcend" refers to the fruits of the world and non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), all of which are described as "vast.
The subsequent phrase, "the three," also uses the Sanskrit term *samyaksambodhi*, which is translated here as "perfect enlightenment."
It is solely the unsurpassed fruit.
By bestowing virtue upon sentient beings, it causes them to attain two superior paths within the causal stage,
and causes them to obtain the fruits of their own respective vehicles at the stage of fruition.
This summarizes the meaning of the four lines.
The first line refers to the merit of composing this treatise;
the second line formally dedicates that merit to sentient beings.
The final two lines below are intended to cause one to attain the fruit [of Buddhahood], to depart from the state of an ordinary person, and to become a sage.

This concludes the *Commentary on the Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra* (Jūchūron Juki), Volume Lower. It was transcribed from the sixteenth day of the seventh month to the twentieth day of the same month in the fifth year of Enpō (the *Mushin* year, 1678). The total number of sheets is sixty-three. This was done both as an offering of gratitude for divine grace and as a prayer that all spirits may be freed from suffering. From the fourth day of this month to the seventeenth day of this month, at the various halls of Kōfuku-ji, three scrolls—upper, middle, and lower—were transcribed and respectfully enshrined in the main lecture hall (*dangiya*). Those with sincere hearts should recite the *Komyō Shingon* (Light Mantra) six times and chant the Name.
The śramaṇa Jinchun increased his devotion in the spring of the thirty-third year.
*Namu* to the Bodhisattva of Compassion and Myriad Practices. Nanto.
